scenes.say: Six bytes of data, and size of says twelve. Where did the other six go? By the end, you'll shrink that struct by a third, and build an object in memory you already own.
Today you will do three things. See why a struct is bigger than its fields add up to. Reorder the fields to shrink it. And build an object in memory you already own, with no allocation.
lines: See why a struct outgrows its fields
Build an object in memory you own

scenes.title: Why is sizeof 12, not 6?
scenes.statement: A struct holds a char, an int and a char: six bytes of data. Explain its size.

example.input: struct { char a; int b; char c; }

scenes.say: A char, an int, a char: six bytes of data. Ask size of, and it says twelve. Who added six bytes? Padding is unused filler the compiler inserts. Typical platform: an int is four bytes.

scenes.head: A shelf with four-slot boxes
scenes.say: Picture a shelf of single slots. Each slot is one byte of memory. An int is a box four slots wide. It may only start at slot zero, four, or eight. That is alignment. A char is one slot: it fits anywhere.

scenes.head: struct A, byte by byte
scenes.say: Now the real struct. Char a goes first, at offset zero. The int needs a multiple of four, and offset one is not. So the compiler adds three bytes of padding. Then the int lands at four through seven. Char c sits at eight. Then three more padding bytes. Why? In an array, the next struct's int must stay aligned. Twelve bytes in total, six wasted. That answers the card: those gaps are six bytes of padding.

items.text: struct A { char a; int b; char c; }

scenes.say: Your turn. Same machine, but this struct has the int first, then one char. How many bytes? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: What is the size of `struct { int b; char a; }`?

scenes.head: Eight, and here is the proof
scenes.say: Eight. The int takes four bytes, the char one, and padding rounds it up. Here is the code. A is twelve, D is eight. Align of int is four. And a struct takes its largest member's alignment, so align of A is four too.

scenes.title: Shrink it without losing a field
scenes.statement: A game stores a million small structs. Each wastes padding. Keep every field, but make it smaller.

example.input: { char a; int b; char c; } is 12 bytes
example.output: { int b; char a; char c; } is 8 bytes

scenes.say: Same three fields, different order, and the struct drops to eight bytes. Picture a game with a million of these: four megabytes saved for free. How?

scenes.head: struct B: biggest first
scenes.say: Put the int first, at offset zero to three. The two chars follow at four and five, with no gap. The data ends at six, but the size must be a multiple of four. So two padding bytes. Eight in total, two wasted, down from six. That answers the card: biggest first, eight bytes.

items.text: struct B { int b; char a; char c; }

scenes.head: 1,000 structs in an array
scenes.say: Does that matter? Make a thousand of them. Struct A costs twelve thousand bytes. Struct B costs eight thousand. Four kilobytes saved, a third, by reordering alone.
Your turn. A char, an int, a short, and another char. Reorder them as cleverly as you like. What is the smallest size? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: Biggest alignment first
scenes.say: Eight. In the original order, the int jumps to four, the short to eight: twelve. Sorted, int, short, char, char add up to exactly eight, with zero padding. The rule of thumb: biggest alignment first.

scenes.head: Why the hardware cares
scenes.say: Why bother? A cache line is the 64-byte block the CPU fetches. Loads from aligned addresses are usually fastest. Misaligned ones can be slow or fault. In C plus plus, they are undefined. Align as sixty four gives a counter its own cache line. Two threads writing nearby counters slow each other down. That is false sharing. Pragma pack removes padding, at a cost in speed and safety.
rows: slow, may fault, UB in C++
threads slow each other on one line

scenes.title: Make an object without allocating
scenes.statement: You own a buffer of raw bytes. Build a `struct Point { int x, y; }` inside it, then clean it up. new must not allocate.
scenes.say: You already own eight raw bytes on the stack. Can you build a Point, one and two, right inside them? With no heap allocation at all.

scenes.head: Renting vs furnishing
scenes.say: Normal new does two jobs. First it allocates memory, like renting a flat. Then it constructs the object, like moving the furniture in. Placement new skips the renting. You hand it an address you already own.

scenes.head: new (buf) Point{1, 2}
scenes.say: First, reserve raw bytes, sized and aligned with align as for a Point. No object exists yet. Then new, with buf in parentheses, allocates nothing. It runs the constructor there, and hands back a pointer. The bytes now hold one and two. When we finish, we call the destructor ourselves. That answers the card: Point built in buf, with no allocation.

items.label: buf: raw bytes on the stack

scenes.head: The destructor is your job
scenes.say: Here is a class that announces itself. We reserve an aligned buffer, build a Tracer in it with placement new, then call the destructor by hand. Placement new prints ctor. The explicit call prints dtor.
Your turn. Same program, but delete the last line, the destructor call. What does it print? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: `t->~Tracer();` is deleted. What does the program print?

scenes.head: Forget it and dtor never runs
scenes.say: Just ctor. The buffer is a plain array, so nothing calls the destructor. Whatever the object owned, a file or heap memory, leaks. Cleanup is your job.

panels.label: no destructor call

scenes.head: Three ways it goes wrong
scenes.say: Three traps. Delete it, and you free memory new never allocated: undefined behavior. Skip the destructor, and resources leak. Give it a buffer that is too small or misaligned, and that is undefined behavior too.

scenes.head: Where placement new lives
scenes.say: You will not write it often, but you use it daily. Vector reserves raw capacity, then builds each element in place. Optional keeps raw storage, and builds the value only when set. Memory pools place many objects in one big block.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: What is alignment? Types start at multiples of their alignment. Padding fills gaps. Example? Char, int, char is twelve. Shrink it? Biggest first gives eight. Why care? Misaligned access is slow or undefined.
rows: start at a multiple of `alignof`; padding fills gaps

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: What is placement new? It constructs an object at an address you supply, without allocating. Cleanup? You call the destructor yourself, and never delete. Requirements? Big enough, properly aligned. Where is it used? Vector, optional, and memory pools.
rows: constructs at your address, no allocation

scenes.head: Practice before your interview
scenes.say: Try these three. Print size of and offset of every field in a struct of your own. Reorder until the padding is as small as you can get it. Then placement new a string into an aligned buffer, and destroy it by hand.
rows: see the padding with your own eyes

scenes.say: So say this. Alignment means types start at multiples of their alignment. Order fields biggest first to shrink a struct. Placement new builds an object at your address, and you destroy it yourself.
lines: Order biggest first to shrink a struct.
Placement new: construct there, destroy by hand.
